blocks.title: Molar volume
blocks.text: The volume of one mole of an ideal gas at STP (standard temperature and pressure) is called the molar volume, Vm. Its value is 22.414 dm3, commonly rounded to 22.4 dm3.

Using the molar volume, the mass or moles of a gas at STP can be converted into volume and vice versa. According to Avogadro's law, equal volumes of all ideal gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules. This is indirectly the same as saying that one mole of an ideal gas at 273.16 K and one atmosphere has a volume of 22.414 dm3; since one mole has Avogadro's number of particles, 22.414 dm3 of any ideal gas at STP holds 6.02 x 10^23 molecules. So 22.4 dm3 of a gas at STP = the molar mass of the gas = 6.02 x 10^23 particles = 1 mole. If the number of moles of a gas is known, its volume is the number of moles multiplied by the molar volume: V = n x Vm.
